people.summary: Japanese social life runs on quiet consideration of others. Expect politeness by default, low public volume, strict queueing, punctuality, and mutual privacy. Visitors earn a lot of goodwill by matching that register.

traits.title: Quiet in public
traits.body: Phone calls on trains are considered rude. Keep voices low in restaurants and shrines.

traits.title: Queueing is sacred
traits.body: Lines form for trains (at the marked floor stripes), elevators, food stalls, and even for pressing the walk button at some crossings. Never jump a queue.

traits.title: Bowing as greeting
traits.body: A short nod works for tourists. Handshakes are fine in business; don't both bow and shake at once. Don't kiss on the cheek.

traits.title: Punctuality
traits.body: Trains leave to the second. If you're 10 minutes late for a reservation, call ahead or risk forfeiting the table.

traits.title: Gift-giving
traits.body: A small wrapped gift (omiyage) from your home country is a thoughtful gesture for a host, guide, or friend. Hand over with two hands.

traits.title: Shoes off
traits.body: Remove shoes at private homes, ryokan, many temples' inner halls, some restaurants (watch for a raised entryway called a genkan and a shoe cubby).

traits.title: Cash etiquette
traits.body: Place cash or cards on the small tray at the register rather than handing directly to the cashier. They'll do the same when giving change.

traits.title: Saying no
traits.body: Direct refusal is rare. 'Chotto muzukashii' (a little difficult) or a sharp intake of breath often means 'no'.

traits.title: Tattoos
traits.body: Tattoos still carry yakuza associations for older generations — covered in onsen, gyms, and some pools. Many tattoo-friendly spots now exist; check ahead.

traits.title: Photos of people
traits.body: Ask before photographing individuals, especially geisha in Gion and shrine visitors in ceremonial dress. Some alleys in Gion now ban photography outright.

dress_codes.label: Temples and shrines
dress_codes.notes: Shoulders and knees covered inside main halls. Loose, comfortable clothing works. Shoes must come off at the entrance to inner halls.

dress_codes.label: Onsen (hot spring bath)
dress_codes.notes: Bathing is done nude — swimwear is not allowed. You bring a small modesty towel. Shower thoroughly before entering the pool.

dress_codes.label: Upscale restaurant
dress_codes.notes: Michelin and fine-dining venues expect collared shirts / blouses, long trousers or a dress. Shorts, beach sandals, and tank tops will usually be turned away.

dress_codes.label: Clubs (Shibuya / Roppongi)
dress_codes.notes: Doormen often refuse athletic wear, shorts, and sandals. Sneakers are fine as long as they're clean.

dress_codes.label: Business meetings
dress_codes.notes: Suit and tie for men, conservative business attire for women. Bring a business-card holder for meishi (cards) exchanged with two hands.

dress_codes.label: Day-to-day sightseeing
dress_codes.notes: Anything clean and comfortable. Tokyoites dress up more than many Western cities — trainers are fine but very revealing clothing stands out.
